name: Leucine
lead: Leucine is an essential branched-chain amino acid (BCAA): the human body cannot make it, so it must come from dietary protein such as meat, dairy, eggs, soy and legumes [1]. Together with isoleucine and valine it is one of the three BCAAs [32], and it is sold both as a stand-alone powder and as an ingredient in BCAA, essential amino acid, protein and pre- or intra-workout products.

For appearance, leucine's relevance runs through muscle. Lifters build the shoulders, back, arms and legs that define a physique by training and by supplying enough amino acids for muscle protein synthesis, and leucine is the amino acid most often singled out as the signal that switches that process on through the mTORC1 pathway [1][13][33]. The chain that bodybuilding communities describe is: leucine-rich protein or supplement, then stronger mTORC1 signalling, then more muscle protein built after training, then a larger, fuller physique over months.

Human trials show that protein supplementation in general modestly increases gains in lean mass and strength during resistance training [3]. Whether adding isolated leucine or BCAAs to an already adequate protein intake produces further gains in healthy trainees is debated among researchers, with some short trials reporting a rise in post-exercise muscle protein synthesis [38] and a review arguing that BCAAs alone cannot support a full anabolic response without the other essential amino acids [37]. Most clinical work on leucine-enriched products has been done in older adults with sarcopenia, with mixed results [5][7].

paras: Leucine is taken mainly by people who lift weights or who want to preserve lean mass, either as free-form L-leucine or inside whey protein, BCAA blends and essential amino acid products. Because whey and casein are rich in leucine, many forum discussions treat dietary protein quality as a proxy for leucine content, and some posters argue that soy protein is less effective than whey in part because of its lower leucine content [31].

The International Society of Sports Nutrition's position stand on protein and exercise lists leucine within its guidance for resistance-trained people: it describes roughly 0.25 g/kg of high-quality protein, or 20 to 40 g, per serving, with each serving ideally providing about 700 to 3,000 mg of leucine, spaced every three to four hours, and pre-sleep casein as a way to raise overnight muscle protein synthesis [35]. Leucine content is the reason whey, which is rich in it, features so prominently in physique-oriented diets.
Clinically, leucine-enriched formulas are studied as nutritional support in sarcopenia (age-related muscle loss), frailty and muscle disuse [7][8][9][11].

BCAA products that include leucine are also used before or during training, mainly in the hope of reducing soreness and supporting recovery. A 2017 meta-analysis cited by Wikipedia's BCAA article suggested that BCAA supplementation may lower creatine kinase and reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness after exercise, and a 2019 systematic review reported possible reductions in muscle lactic acid during exercise [32]. Better recovery is the chain by which this could lead to more training and more muscle.

A 2018 meta-analysis of 49 randomised trials (1,863 participants) found that protein supplementation during at least six weeks of resistance training produced small average increases in strength, fat-free mass and muscle cross-sectional area, with the effect on fat-free mass smaller with increasing age and larger in resistance-trained people [3]. This analysis concerns total protein, not leucine in isolation.

A 12-week randomised trial in men and women compared soy and whey protein supplements that were matched for leucine content and reported no significant differences in muscle growth or strength [10]. Researchers and forum participants cite this kind of result in discussions of whether leucine content explains differences between protein sources.

The Wikipedia article notes that results of studies on supplemental leucine are conflicting and that long-term supplementation has not been shown to raise muscle mass or strength in healthy elderly men [1].

Leucine's reputation as the key muscle-building amino acid grew out of cell biology rather than bodybuilding. Early rat diaphragm experiments, summarised in a review of BCAA research, found that a BCAA mixture stimulated muscle protein synthesis about as well as a complete amino acid mixture, and that leucine alone produced nearly the same effect as the full BCAA set, while isoleucine or valine alone did little [32].

The pathway involved is built around mTOR. The kinase's target protein was identified in 1994 as the direct target of rapamycin, a compound isolated from soil bacteria collected during the 1964 to 1965 Easter Island medical expedition and reported by Surendra Nath Sehgal in 1972 [33]. Researchers later described mTORC1 as a complex that senses nutrients and controls protein synthesis, and listed leucine among the amino acids that activate it [33]. Sestrin2 (2016) and SAR1B (2021) were reported as proteins that sense leucine and feed into mTORC1 [13][14].

Human studies translated this into exercise physiology. Reviews describe how contraction and amino acids separately regulate mTORC1 signalling and protein synthesis in human muscle [15], and a 2006 study cited by the BCAA article reported that leucine infusion at rest kept muscle protein synthesis elevated for up to six hours [32]. mTORC1 activation is described as required for muscle growth after exercise and after intake of certain amino acids [33].

sections.h: Leucine in physique and sports nutrition
paras: In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding discussions the practical questions are how much leucine a meal supplies, whether a protein source is leucine-rich, and whether extra free leucine or BCAAs add anything. The ISSN position stand frames a leucine amount per serving as part of an effective protein dose, not as a replacement for total protein, which it puts at about 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg per day for most exercising people [35].

Protein-source comparisons are the other common thread. In a 2009 study of young men given 10 g of essential amino acids as whey, casein or soy, whey raised blood leucine most and produced the largest rise in muscle protein synthesis after resistance exercise; the authors attributed the differences mainly to digestion speed and possibly to small leucine differences [36]. A later 12-week trial that matched soy and whey for leucine found no significant differences in muscle growth or strength [10].

A 2017 study in ten resistance-trained men reported that 5.6 g of BCAAs after exercise raised myofibrillar protein synthesis by about 22 percent over placebo, with greater phosphorylation of mTORC1 targets [38]. A narrative review the same year argued that BCAAs alone could raise synthesis by at most about 30 percent, and that no human study had measured the effect of oral BCAAs alone on synthesis in a way that supports a full anabolic claim [37]. These two papers are often cited on opposite sides of the BCAA discussion.

Leucine is a normal dietary component. In decompensated maple syrup urine disease, a genetic disorder of branched-chain amino acid metabolism, leucine accumulation causes delirium and neurological compromise and can be life-threatening [1].

High leucine intake has been proposed to worsen pellagra in people with low niacin status, because it interferes with conversion of tryptophan to niacin, and intakes above about 500 mg/kg/day have been associated with raised blood ammonia; an unofficial upper level of about 35 g/day for healthy men under acute conditions has been suggested [1].

Elevated circulating BCAAs, including leucine, are associated with insulin resistance and with future type 2 diabetes risk in observational metabolomic studies [6]. Whether this reflects cause, effect or a marker of other metabolic changes is not established by those studies. Reports from users and gastrointestinal complaints at high doses are discussed informally; one T Nation poster notes that straight leucine powder is difficult to dissolve [28].

Maple syrup urine disease is a rare autosomal recessive condition, affecting about 1 in 185,000 births worldwide, in which the enzyme complex that breaks down BCAAs is deficient; accumulated leucine and its by-products are toxic to the brain, and treatment involves lifelong protein restriction and monitored formulas [34]. In 2025 the European Medicines Agency approved a prescription BCAA product for acute episodes in these patients, a medical use unrelated to supplementation [32]. Mouse studies reported a shortened lifespan with BCAA supplementation alone, while another mouse study of a BCAA-enriched essential amino acid mixture reported extended lifespan, and a link between BCAA-containing sports supplements and ALS has been suggested but not established [32].

Leucine directly stimulates myofibrillar protein synthesis by activating mTOR, a kinase that regulates protein synthesis and cell growth. The activation involves Rag GTPases, leucyl-tRNA synthetase and the sensor Sestrin2, and possibly other mechanisms [1]. Sestrin2 was described in 2016 as a leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway [13], and in 2021 SAR1B was reported as another leucine-sensing protein [14].
Reviews of human muscle physiology describe how nutrients and muscle contraction both regulate protein synthesis and mTORC1 signalling [15].

Most dietary leucine is handled in the liver, fat and muscle. Around 60% is metabolised within several hours, about 40% ends up as acetyl-CoA, and roughly 5% (range 2 to 10%) is converted to beta-hydroxy beta-methylbutyrate (HMB), a minor metabolite also sold as a supplement [1]. Leucine is one of only two exclusively ketogenic amino acids [1].

Leucine is an aliphatic alpha-amino acid with an isobutyl side chain (formula C6H13NO2) [1][2]. The name derives from the Greek for 'white'. According to Grokipedia, it was first isolated from cheese in 1819 by Joseph Louis Proust and from wool and muscle in 1820 by Henri Braconnot [2]; this account has not been checked against a primary source.

Trials of leucine in humans fall into a few groups. In older adults with sarcopenia, a meta-analysis of three studies (637 patients) of whey protein, leucine and vitamin D combinations found no significant difference in grip strength or short physical performance battery scores overall, but appendicular muscle mass improved; with a concurrent exercise programme, grip strength and performance scores improved [5].

The PROVIDE trial, a multicentre double-blind randomised study, tested a vitamin D and leucine-enriched whey supplement in older adults with sarcopenia [7]. A two-month randomised trial of a food containing 2.5 g leucine, omega-3 fatty acids and a probiotic strain in older people with sarcopenia also reported on lean mass, performance and inflammation [8]. A de-training follow-up trial examined leucine-enriched whey with resistance training over 24 weeks [9], and further randomised trials tested multi-component supplements for frailty and for rehabilitation in sarcopenia [11][12]. Because these products combine leucine with other ingredients, they do not isolate leucine's own effect.
An umbrella review of nutritional interventions in people aged 65 and over assessed supplementation across several muscle outcomes [4].

Registered trials on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of leucine dose and muscle maintenance during weight loss (NCT07583875), leucine to offset disuse atrophy (NCT03762278), leucine in older-age anabolic responses (NCT06567665), leucine requirements, and leucine in Diamond Blackfan anemia [16][17][18][19][20].

timeline.event: Leucine is first isolated from cheese by Joseph Louis Proust, according to Grokipedia [2].
Henri Braconnot obtains it from hydrolysed wool and muscle [2].
Rapamycin, later found to target mTOR, is isolated from soil bacteria by Surendra Nath Sehgal [33].
Several groups identify mTOR as rapamycin's direct target in mammalian cells [33].
The US Food and Nutrition Board sets an RDA for essential amino acids, including leucine [1].
A study of whey, casein and soy finds the largest post-exercise muscle protein synthesis response with whey [36].
Sestrin2 is reported as a leucine sensor for mTORC1 [13].
The ISSN protein position stand gives a per-serving leucine range; a BCAA trial and a critical BCAA review are published [35][37][38].
A 49-study meta-analysis quantifies the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training gains [3].
SAR1B is reported as a leucine sensor regulating mTORC1 [14].
The European Medicines Agency approves a prescription BCAA product for acute maple syrup urine disease episodes [32].

lore.intro: On T Nation, leucine is discussed as the 'key amino acid for muscle protein synthesis' and as a component of pre-workout formulas, with debate about whether stand-alone leucine or BCAAs add anything beyond whole protein [24][28][29].

claims.claim: Leucine 'turns on' mTOR and is the key trigger for muscle growth
claims.believers: Forum posts and articles describe leucine as the amino acid that activates mTOR and maintains or increases muscle, and recommend leucine-rich whey and casein for this reason [24][29].
claims.experts: Laboratory studies confirm leucine-sensing pathways that feed mTORC1 [13][14], and the mechanism is described in reference works [1]. Whether supplementing extra leucine raises long-term muscle gain in well-fed healthy people is not established [1].

claims.claim: Soy protein is inferior to whey because of lower leucine content
claims.believers: A T Nation thread on soy notes that soy was inferior to whey in a cited study and attributes this to differences in quality, digestibility and leucine content [31].
claims.experts: A 12-week trial that matched soy and whey supplements for leucine found no significant differences in muscle growth or strength [10].

claims.claim: Adding leucine to a pre- or post-workout drink offers extra benefit
claims.believers: Users of a commercial workout formula that contains 5 g of leucine ask or report on what leucine and malic acid add, and some describe the product as working well [26][27].
claims.experts: No published trial has tested that specific formula; trials of leucine-enriched products have largely been in older adults with sarcopenia and combine leucine with other nutrients [5][7].

claims.claim: Leucine alone, not BCAA blends, is what matters (or BCAAs are not needed if protein is adequate)
claims.believers: One poster tells others to drop BCAAs and rely on whole animal proteins and eggs, saying protein itself drives insulin and meeting daily protein matters more than timing [30].
claims.experts: The 2018 meta-analysis supports a benefit of total protein supplementation during resistance training [3]; direct comparisons of leucine against BCAA products in trained people are not reported in the cited literature.

claims.claim: BCAAs taken on their own build muscle
claims.believers: Supporters point to a study in which BCAAs after training raised muscle protein synthesis by roughly 22 percent [38].
claims.experts: A review argues the oral BCAA effect alone is capped and that the other essential amino acids are needed for full synthesis [37].

claims.claim: You only need a little protein if it is leucine rich
claims.believers: A T Nation poster notes research showing small amounts of leucine-rich protein can stimulate protein synthesis, while also saying a well-formed diet needs more than that [39].
claims.experts: The ISSN position stand describes 20 to 40 g of protein per serving, with leucine part of that dose, and 1.4 to 2.0 g/kg per day for most exercising people [35].

claims.claim: BCAAs speed recovery and cut soreness
claims.believers: Users and supplement formulas pair BCAAs with training in the hope of feeling less sore and recovering faster.
claims.experts: A 2017 meta-analysis summarised in the BCAA article suggested lower creatine kinase and less delayed-onset muscle soreness after exercise [32].

angle.text: People who lift use leucine, mostly through leucine-rich whey and casein or through BCAA and pre-workout products, to support the muscle building that drives a fuller, more muscular physique. The effect on looks comes through added lean mass when combined with resistance training and adequate total protein.
